topic: Pegloticase and lesinurad in refractory gout: indications, infusion reactions
synopsis: The 2020 ACR gout guideline strongly recommends against pegloticase as first-line urate-lowering therapy. Switching to pegloticase, rather than continuing the current urate-lowering drug, is strongly recommended when xanthine oxidase inhibitors, uricosurics, and other interventions have failed to reach the serum-urate target and the patient still has frequent flares (at least 2 per year) or non-resolving subcutaneous tophi. The same switch is strongly recommended against when flares are infrequent (fewer than 2 per year) and there are no tophi. Trial populations had at least 3 flares in 18 months, at least one tophus, or gouty arthropathy, plus allopurinol contraindication or failure to normalize uric acid after at least 3 months at the maximum medically appropriate dose. Benefits in serum urate, flares, tophi, and quality of life came with high cost, twice-monthly infusions, and the potential for serious allergic reactions. Lesinurad was withdrawn from the US market by the manufacturer while the guideline was being written; it remained FDA-approved, so the panel still considered its data.

teachingPoints.claim: Pegloticase is strongly recommended against as first-line therapy.
teachingPoints.sourceExcerpt: pegloticase as a first-line therapy is strongly recommended against.

teachingPoints.claim: Pegloticase is strongly recommended after XOI, uricosuric, and other failure when flares are frequent or tophi persist.
teachingPoints.sourceExcerpt: Switching to pegloticase over continuing current ULT is strongly recommended for patients with gout for whom XOI treatment, uricosurics, and other interventions have failed to achieve the SU target, and who continue to have frequent gout flares (≥2 flares/year) OR who have nonresolving subcutaneous tophi.

teachingPoints.claim: Serious allergic reactions and twice-monthly infusions are explicit harms.
teachingPoints.sourceExcerpt: these outcomes come with high costs, twice-monthly infusions, and the potential for serious allergic reactions.

uncertaintiesNotedInSource: Lesinurad dosing is not restated as a current US starting regimen because the drug was withdrawn from the US market during guideline development.
